title: Why Arribes tastes the way it does

lede.text: Vines here grow in a granite canyon about 5°C warmer than the plateau above it. The warmth ripens the grapes fully and gives the wines a certain lean towards overripe, stewed fruit. Rain that comes in time keeps their natural acidity fresh.

chapters.title: A canyon cut into the plateau
paras: The land drops from about 700 m on the plateau to only 130 m at the riverbanks within a few kilometres. The Duero and the Tormes cut this canyon into a granite base, along with smaller rivers such as the Uces and the Huebra. These slopes are the arribes. It is not a mountain zone, but the drops are large and the hillsides are many.
The plateau is called the penillanura. The canyon walls and the plateau give the vines two different climates.

fly.label: The Arribes canyon
fly.caption: The Duero and its tributaries cut a canyon into the granite, from about 700 m down to 130 m.

chapters.title: The warmest corner of Castilla y León
paras: This is the westernmost end of the Duero basin, so rain is relatively high: 575 to 800 mm a year. The climate is sub-humid Mediterranean, warmer and wetter than the rest of the region. Average temperatures here are the highest in all of Castilla y León. The low altitude and the Atlantic influence explain it, helped by the microclimate of the valleys.

On the plateau the winters are long and cold and the summers short and hot. In the river valleys it is about 5°C warmer. The winters there are shorter and the summers longer. Frost is not known in the canyons. January averages about 9°C and August about 26°C, with about 2,680 hours of sun a year. The valleys also bring more sun and shelter from cold winds.

The spring comes early and the rain arrives in time, so the natural acidity does not usually fall below 5.5 g/l. The warmth ripens the grapes fully and concentrates the polyphenols. The wines show a certain lean towards overripe, stewed fruit.

chapters.title: Thin, stony granite
paras: The base rock is granite, with some slate. The soils are silty sand and very stony. The soils are generally shallow, about 30 cm on average, a little deeper over slate.

The soil is a pale yellow-brown. It is acid, with a pH of 5 to 6, and poor in lime. It holds little organic matter, 1.5 to 3%. Juan García, the main red grape, thrives even on the poorest ground and gives steady yields. It gives the wines structure and softness.

chapters.title: Old bush vines and the barrel
paras: At least half of the vineyard was planted before 1956. Almost all of it is bush-trained. Traditional planting density is 2,000 to 3,000 vines per hectare. Trellised vines are rare.
Phylloxera came from Portugal and entered the region through the Arribes in 1888. By about 1913-14 the vineyards were recovering, and red grapes came to dominate.

A wine labelled Fermentado en Barrica (barrel-fermented) is both fermented and aged on its lees in oak barrels of 600 l at most, for at least three months. It shows smoky, toasty notes mixed with fruity or floral aromas, and well-blended oak.
The whites are fruity or floral, sometimes with a mineral note. The reds are rich in polyphenols with ripe fruit aromas.

fly.label: Fermoselle
fly.caption: Fermoselle is one of the towns where the vineyards recovered fully after phylloxera, by about 1913-14.

terms.text: A rosé or red that has spent at least three months in oak barrels.
